1415.title: Clay jars (2 Corinthians 4:7–9)
1415.hook: treasure in clay jars: pressed but not crushed
1415.howItsDone: Some Christians return to the clay jars passage in times of illness, burnout or loss, and some churches and ministries use a clay jar or a broken pot with a light inside as a picture of God's power in human weakness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's list: beaten, shipwrecked, cold, and lowered from a wall in a basket. Your line was still here.

Where would you keep something priceless? A safe. A vault. A velvet box with a lock. Not, probably, in the chipped mug by the sink. And yet that's where Paul says God keeps it. Same letter as yesterday's list, a few chapters earlier. Paul has been talking about light, and faces, and what God has put inside ordinary people. Then he reaches for the plainest object in any house, the clay pot that cracks if you drop it, and says: that's us.
screen: `A SAFE, A VAULT, A VELVET BOX.`
`OR THE CHIPPED MUG BY THE SINK.`

segments.voice: First, the treasure, in the King James words: "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts." Some readers hear an echo of let there be light: the God who lit the world has lit something inside people. Then the jar: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." Earthen vessels. Clay jars. Paul doesn't pretend the jar is strong. The weakness is the point: if the jar is ordinary, nobody mistakes where the light comes from. Then life in a clay jar, in four pairs: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." Each pair has the same shape: a blow, and then a but not. In plainer words, pressed, but not crushed. Knocked down, but not finished. Paul never says the blows don't land. They do. They just don't get the last inch. Some readers hear an echo of Gideon in Judges, whose small band carried empty pitchers with lamps hidden inside; at the signal they broke the pitchers, and the light shone out in the dark. Paul doesn't mention Gideon, so that's a connection readers make. But it fits. A clay jar isn't a failure of the treasure. It's where the treasure lives.
screen: `A BLOW, AND THEN A BUT NOT.`

segments.voice: If there's a mug or a bowl near you, pick it up, or cup your empty hands, and feel how plain it is: the chip, the stain, the crack in the glaze. Think of yourself the way Paul thinks of the jar, not polished, not unbreakable, still carrying something, and name one place you feel pressed right now, then quietly say the other half: but not crushed. If you pray, you can thank God for the light in an ordinary jar.
Clay jars. Paul's picture of ordinary, breakable people carrying God's light, so the power is plainly God's. Troubled, but not distressed.
Your line: pressed, not crushed. In Paul's picture, the cracks don't disqualify the jar. Go gently.

1416.title: Light affliction (2 Corinthians 4:16–18)
1416.hook: outwardly wasting, inwardly renewed day by day
1416.howItsDone: Some Christians read 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 at funerals, in hospitals and in seasons of aging or illness, as words about an inner life renewed while the body wears out, and about a hope beyond what is seen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, clay jars: treasure in earthen vessels. Your line was pressed, not crushed.

Light. That's Paul's word for his troubles. Light. This is the man whose list we read two days ago: beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked, hungry, cold, lowered from a city wall in a basket. Later in this very letter he'll write that list down. And here, a few verses after the clay jars, he calls it all light affliction. A friend who said that about a year like that might get a worried phone call. So either Paul is in denial, or he's weighing his troubles against something so heavy that they really do feel light.

Here are the lines, in the King James words: "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Two people in one body. The outward one is wearing out, and Paul doesn't hide it: knees, eyes, energy, the face in the mirror. The inward one is being made new, and not once. Day by day. Then the weighing: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." Hear it as a balance scale. On one side, the affliction: real, but light, and only for a moment. On the other, glory: a weight, and eternal. Paul isn't saying the suffering is small. He's saying it's small next to what it sits beside. Then the last line says where to look: "the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." Temporal means for a time. The hospital bracelet, the bills, the gray hair: real, and all for a time. Some readers hear a promise about the life to come; some also hear something happening now, a little each day, an inner life renewed while the outer one tires. Not a single dramatic rescue. Just today, and then today again.

Notice your outward self first, whatever aches or is tired, and let it be tired without judging it. Then turn inward and ask what would make the inner person a little newer today: not a whole new life, just one small thing, a short walk, a psalm read slowly, a call to someone who makes you laugh, an early night. If you pray, you can ask God for today's renewal, just today's.
Light affliction. Paul's name for real suffering, weighed against an eternal weight of glory, while the inward self is renewed day by day.
Your line: renewed day by day. The outward self tires; the inward one is being made new. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1417.title: Comforted to comfort (2 Corinthians 1:3–4)
1417.hook: the God of all comfort comforts us so we can comfort others
1417.howItsDone: Christians comfort one another through visits, meals, prayer and simply sitting with people who grieve, and some churches run grief groups or care teams in which people who have been through a loss support others going through the same.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the outward self wearing out, the inward one made new. Your line was renewed day by day.

Two women at a kitchen table. One lost her husband last month, and the house is full of flowers she doesn't know what to do with. The other lost hers years ago. She doesn't make a speech. She knows which casseroles freeze well. She knows the second month can be harder than the first, when the cards stop coming. She knows not to say he's in a better place unless she's asked. She learned it at her own kitchen table, from someone who sat with her. Paul has a line for exactly this.
screen: `SHE LEARNED IT AT HER OWN TABLE.`

segments.voice: It's how Paul opens his second letter to Corinth, the letter of the past few days. In the King James words: "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God." Count the comfort words: comfort, comforteth, comfort, comfort, comforted. Five, in two verses. It starts with God, the God of all comfort. It reaches us in all our tribulation. And it doesn't stop there: that we may be able to comfort others. Comfort, in this letter, isn't a pool you sit in. It's a river. It comes in so it can go out. Paul isn't writing from a calm desk, either. A few verses later he says that in Asia they were "pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life." So this comfort isn't advice from someone who's never been under it. It's been tested. That's why the widow at the kitchen table helps. Not because she suffered, as if suffering were the qualification, but because she was comforted, and remembers how it was done. Some readers see in this a picture of how a church works: the comforted becoming comforters, so no one's comfort ends with them.

Remember a time someone comforted you, who it was and what they actually did, maybe food, or silence, or a text on the hard date without being asked. Then think of someone going through something like what you went through, and picture that same comfort passed on to them; if you pray, you can name them before God. And if you're in a stretch where even life feels too heavy, you don't have to carry it alone: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Comforted to comfort. Paul's picture of God's comfort as a river: it reaches us in our trouble so it can reach others in theirs.
Your line: pass the comfort on. It starts, Paul writes, with the God of all comfort. See you tomorrow.

1418.title: The darkness is not dark (Psalm 139:11–12)
1418.hook: the night shines as the day to you
1418.howItsDone: Christians pray Psalm 139 in personal prayer and in worship, and in churches that pray night prayer, evening psalms and prayers ask for God's presence through the dark hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the God of all comfort, and comfort that keeps moving like a river. Your line was pass the comfort on.

The power goes out. The fridge stops humming, the screens die, and the room you know by heart becomes a room you don't. You reach for the wall. A chair leg finds your shin. An old song goes right into that moment, and further, into the other kinds of dark: the sleepless hours before dawn, the year nobody could see the way through. It's a psalm whose heading names David, and in the middle of it the singer says something strange about the dark.

Psalm 139 starts with being known: "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me." Then it turns into a kind of hide and seek, and the singer tries every hiding place. "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there." Up, down. Then the wings of the morning, the uttermost parts of the sea. Even there. And then the last hiding place, the dark. In the King James words: "If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me. Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." Readers hear the singer two ways here. Some hear someone hoping the dark will hide them. Others hear someone afraid it will swallow them whole. Notice where the light comes from. No dawn arrives, no lamp is lit. The night is light about the singer because the night isn't dark to God, who sees in it as in the day. A few lines later the psalm goes to one more dark place, the womb, where, it says, I was made in secret. The singer's life began in the dark, and God was there too. So for those who pray this psalm, the dark may still be dark. But it isn't empty.

Dim the lights or close your eyes, and let the dark be what it is, the sounds that get louder, the edges that disappear; if something in your life feels dark right now, let it come in too, without fixing it. If you pray, say the psalm's line slowly, the darkness and the light are both alike to thee; if not, simply rest here. If the dark ever feels like too much to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
The darkness is not dark. Psalm 139's claim that there is no hiding place from God, not even the night, because the night shineth as the day.

1419.title: The groaning Spirit (Romans 8:26)
1419.hook: when we don't know how to pray, the Spirit groans for us
1419.howItsDone: Christians lean on Romans 8:26 when they can't find words to pray, in grief or illness; some pray in silence, some sigh or weep before God, and some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect it with praying in tongues.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the darkness is not dark: the night shineth as the day. Your line was dark and light alike.

A car parked outside a sister's house, engine off. Someone behind the wheel means to pray before knocking. God, please. Please what? Heal her? Give her peace? Let it be quick? Every request sounds wrong the moment it forms. So no words come. Just a long breath out, from somewhere under the ribs. Then they open the door and walk up the path. Was that a prayer? Paul, writing to the church in Rome, has an answer.

Back on day one hundred six, a dry prayer still counted. Here Paul goes further, in the King James words: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." Notice who admits not knowing. Not a beginner. Paul. Not knowing how to pray isn't a failure here. It's assumed. And notice the sound: groanings which cannot be uttered. Something deeper than words. In this one chapter, three things groan. The first we met on the day about hope: the whole creation, groaning and travailing like a woman in labor. Then us: "even we ourselves groan within ourselves." And then the Spirit, groaning with us and for us. The world aches, we ache, and God's own Spirit takes up the ache and carries it. The next verse says the one who searches the hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, the same searching God of yesterday's psalm. Christians understand these groanings in different ways. Some hear the Spirit's own wordless prayer, beyond anything we say. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect this verse with praying in tongues; other Christians don't read it that way. Whichever reading, the line keeps one comfort at its center: when words run out, the prayer doesn't. The breath in the parked car counts.
screen: `WE KNOW NOT WHAT TO PRAY FOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the thing you don't know how to pray about, a person, or a situation with no good outcome you can name, and don't look for words. Breathe in slowly and let it out as a long sigh with the weight of it inside, then once more. If you pray, let the sigh be the prayer, trusting what Paul says about the Spirit carrying it; if you don't, let it simply be an honest breath that says this matters.
The groaning Spirit. Paul's words for what happens when we don't know how to pray: the Spirit intercedes with groanings which cannot be uttered.

1420.title: Two names on one stone
1420.hook: the Christian hope is that love is stronger than death
1420.carry: not even death separates us from God's love
1420.howItsDone: Christians read Romans 8:38–39 and 1 Corinthians 15 at funerals and on Easter, and the Song of Songs' line about love and death is sometimes read at weddings; some churches also remember the dead by name in their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the groaning Spirit: groanings which cannot be uttered. Your line was the spirit prays.

A gravestone with two names carved on it. One has both dates filled in. The other has the first date, and a blank space after the dash, waiting. Somebody chose that stone. They stood in an office and decided their name would go next to the person they loved, while they're still alive. It's a strange, stubborn thing to do. It says: death has taken one of us, and still hasn't separated us. The Bible has a few lines on that.

Start with a love song. Near the end of the Song of Songs, the beloved says, in the King James words: "Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death." Not stronger. As strong. Even that is daring: death is hard to argue with, and a love poem calls it an even match. Then: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." Later in Romans 8, the groaning Spirit's chapter, Paul lists everything that could cut people off from God's love, and he puts death first: "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Neither death. That's where the Christian hope steps past the love song, from as strong to stronger. The reason Christians give is Easter: the belief that Jesus died and rose, so death didn't have the last say over love. Elsewhere Paul taunts death: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" Churches describe what that hope means for those who have died in different ways, and much of it they leave with God. Love doesn't make death painless. The stone still has a name on it. The hope is that death doesn't get to separate what love has joined to God.

Bring to mind someone you love who is still here, and, if there is one, someone you love who has died, and hold them side by side for a moment, like two names on one stone. If you pray, you can thank God for each of them by name; if you don't, let the love for both simply be there. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Love is stronger. The Song of Songs says love is strong as death. Paul says not even death can separate us from the love of God.

1421.howItsDone: Some churches read the raising of Lazarus in John 11 at funerals or in Lent, and churches encourage sitting with the grieving, visiting the sick, and simply being present, as a way of following Jesus into other people's pain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neither death, nor life, shall be able to separate us from the love of God. Your line was love is stronger.

"Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Two sisters say those exact words to Jesus in John's Gospel. Martha says it on the road. Mary says it at his feet. It's an accusation and a prayer at once, a sentence grief knows: where were you? You could have stopped this. Their brother Lazarus has been in the tomb for days. And what he does next is not what anyone writing a neat answer to suffering would have him do.
screen: `MARTHA ON THE ROAD, MARY AT HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: He doesn't explain. Earlier in the chapter, John has Jesus tell his disciples that Lazarus is asleep and that he is going to wake him. He knows how this ends. Still, when he sees Mary weeping, and the neighbors who came to mourn with her weeping too, the text says he groaned in the spirit and was troubled. The King James uses the same English word, groan, as Romans 8 two days ago, now for Jesus himself. Then one question: "Where have ye laid him?" Not why. Where. Take me to the place it hurts. They say, come and see. Then the verse that in the King James is only two words: "Jesus wept." The people standing there read it the simplest way: "Behold how he loved him!" That's the mystery. Christians have offered reflections on why there is suffering, and some readers say none quite closes the question. What the Gospel gives instead is a God who walks into the grief. John's Gospel opens the same way: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Isaiah said of God and his people: "In all their affliction he was afflicted." Love doesn't stand outside the pain with an explanation. It asks where, and goes there. This week walked through that: clay jars carrying light, affliction weighed against glory, comfort passed on, darkness that isn't dark to God, the Spirit's groan, love stronger than death. And today, the center of it: love that enters.

Bring to mind someone who is hurting, notice the urge to explain or fix it or find the bright side, and set that down. Ask the question Jesus asked, where does it hurt for them, and picture yourself going into that room and sitting down without a speech; if you pray, pray for them simply by name, and if you don't, hold them quietly. If the one hurting is you and it feels like too much, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
The mystery of love. Love that doesn't explain suffering, but enters it: Jesus at the tomb of his friend, asking where, and weeping.
Your line: love enters. At the tomb, Jesus wept. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.

chat.says: If God loves us, why doesn't he just explain why people suffer?
options: At Lazarus's tomb, John shows Jesus asking where, not why, and weeping with them.
John says Jesus explained it all to Martha so she would stop grieving.
John says Jesus stayed away so he wouldn't have to see their grief.
chat.meaning: In John 11, Jesus asks, Where have ye laid him? and weeps. The Gospel shows love that enters grief, not a tidy answer to it.

Lazarus.meaning: brother of Martha and Mary, whose tomb Jesus visits in John

Martha.meaning: Lazarus's sister, who meets Jesus on the road

the Word.meaning: John's name for Jesus at the opening of his Gospel

Isaiah.meaning: a prophet who says God was afflicted in his people's affliction
